most_sensitive.reading: Python computed no sensitivity grid and no scenario values, so which assumption moves value most is not measured here, and I do not rank the drivers by guesswork. What the drivers themselves show is where my three scenarios lie furthest apart against the company's record. The year-ten operating margin runs from below fiscal 2020's {earnings_versus_cash.history.years.5.operating_margin|pct} in the bear case to near fiscal 2023's {earnings_versus_cash.history.years.2.operating_margin|pct} in the bull case. That compares with a trailing margin of {ratios.profitability.operating_margin|pct} and a three-year average of {earnings_versus_cash.history.operating_margin_three_year_average|pct}. Every scenario therefore assumes a margin recovery that the trailing record does not yet show.

most_sensitive.assumption: revenue growth in year one (not measured: Python computed no sensitivity grid)
most_sensitive.reading: Year-one growth is the other driver whose spread across my scenarios covers a wide stretch of the record. The bear case starts with a decline, milder than the fiscal 2024 fall of {earnings_versus_cash.history.years.1.revenue_growth|pct}. The bull case starts a little above the June quarter's {ratios.growth.revenue.year_over_year|pct} and below fiscal 2025's {earnings_versus_cash.history.years.0.revenue_growth|pct}. Growth fades in a straight line to the terminal rate, so the year-one choice carries through all ten years of the forecast. How much value turns on it was not computed.

Some items could not be written as adjustments because the calculator does not carry their amounts: the tariff refunds the release says will not recur, the cut to incentive accruals and the stock-unit reversal, all inside the June quarter.
